claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability.
The combination of low hardness and strength with favorable plasticity and machinability is governed by the absence of significant secondary phases.
The relevant CoCrFeNiTi state is predominantly a single FCC or BCC solid solution.
A uniform single-phase structure with moderate lattice distortion permits relatively easy dislocation motion.
Relatively unimpeded dislocation motion produces lower hardness and strength but higher ductility and machinability.
AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and AlCrFeTiX obtain higher hardness and strength from multiple phases, ordered structures, larger atomic-size mismatch, and/or higher valence-electron concentration.
Multiple phases, ordered structures, or increased lattice distortion impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases hardness and strength, often at the expense of ductility.
Heat treatment or compositional adjustment can induce secondary-phase formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Inducing secondary phases in CoCrFeNiTi will increase its hardness.
Inducing secondary phases in CoCrFeNiTi will increase its strength.
Inducing secondary phases in CoCrFeNiTi will decrease its ductility.
Single-phase CoCrFeNiTi will have lower hardness and strength than multiphase or highly distorted AlCrFeTiX alloys.
Single-phase CoCrFeNiTi will have greater ductility and machinability than multiphase or highly distorted AlCrFeTiX alloys.
The proposed relationships remain valid from 25 °C through 600 °C under tensile or compressive loading up to failure.
If single-phase CoCrFeNiTi has hardness and strength comparable to multiphase AlCrFeTiX without losing ductility, the hypothesis is falsified.
If inducing secondary phases does not increase hardness and strength while reducing ductility, the hypothesis is falsified.

contradictions.description: The intervention and prediction extend the hypothesis to CoCrFeNiTi with significant secondary phases, while the boundary says the hypothesis does not apply to alloys with significant secondary-phase formation.

The comparison is described as controlled, but compositional adjustment or substitution with AlCrFeTiX changes chemistry as well as phase constitution, confounding the proposed phase-mediated effect unless a same-composition heat-treatment comparison is used.
